Proof:
We will construct a minimal uncountable well-ordered set without assuming the Axiom of Choice, following the standard construction of the Hartogs number of the natural numbers.

Let $A = \mathbb{N}$, the set of natural numbers, which is countably infinite. 
Let $W$ be the set of all pairs $(S, R)$ such that $S \subseteq A$ and $R$ is a well-ordering on $S$. 
Since $S \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ and $R \subseteq A \times A$, meaning $R \in \mathcal{P}(A \times A)$, the collection $W$ is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A) \times \mathcal{P}(A \times A)$. By the axioms of power set and specification in ZF, $W$ is a valid set.

We define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $W$ by letting $(S, R) \sim (S', R')$ if and only if the well-ordered sets $(S, R)$ and $(S', R')$ are order-isomorphic. 
Let $\Omega = W / \sim$ be the set of equivalence classes of $\sim$. (Since $W$ is a set, $\Omega$ is a set, formally being a partition of $W$). 
For any $\alpha \in \Omega$, we refer to any $(S, R) \in \alpha$ as a representative of $\alpha$, and $\alpha$ represents the order type of $(S, R)$.

We define a binary relation $\prec$ on $\Omega$ as follows: for $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$, $\alpha \prec \beta$ if and only if for any representative $(S_1, R_1) \in \alpha$ and $(S_2, R_2) \in \beta$, $(S_1, R_1)$ is order-isomorphic to a proper initial segment of $(S_2, R_2)$. 
Since any two well-ordered sets are either isomorphic or one is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of the other, and no well-ordered set is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself, $\prec$ defines a strict total order on $\Omega$. 
Furthermore, $(\Omega, \prec)$ is well-ordered. Indeed, if $X \subseteq \Omega$ is a non-empty subset, pick $\beta \in X$ and a representative $(S_2, R_2) \in \beta$. If $\beta$ is not the least element of $X$, then any $\alpha \in X$ with $\alpha \prec \beta$ corresponds to a unique proper initial segment of $(S_2, R_2)$, which is of the form $\{y \in S_2 : y \mathrel{R_2} x\}$ for some $x \in S_2$. The set of such $x$ for $\alpha \in X$ with $\alpha \prec \beta$ has a least element $x_0$ under $R_2$, which yields the least element of $X$. Thus, $(\Omega, \prec)$ is a well-ordered set.

We now claim that every proper initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable (in the context of the problem statement, 'initial segment in $\Omega$' refers to proper initial segments, since $\Omega$ itself will be shown to be uncountable). 
Let $\beta \in \Omega$ and let $I_\beta = \{ \alpha \in \Omega \mid \alpha \prec \beta \}$ be the strict initial segment determined by $\beta$. 
Choose a representative $(S, R) \in \beta$. By definition, any $\alpha \in I_\beta$ is order-isomorphic to a unique proper initial segment of $(S, R)$. 
The proper initial segments of $(S, R)$ are exactly the sets $S_{<x} = \{ y \in S \mid y \mathrel{R} x \}$ for $x \in S$. 
Thus, the mapping $f: S \to I_\beta$ defined by $f(x) = [(S_{<x}, R|_{S_{<x}})]_\sim$ is a surjection (and in fact, a bijection). 
Since $S \subseteq A = \mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, $S$ is a countable set. 
The existence of a surjection from the countable set $S$ to $I_\beta$ implies that $I_\beta$ is also countable. 
Since $\beta$ was arbitrary, every initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable.

Finally, we show that $\Omega$ itself is uncountable. 
Suppose for contradiction that $\Omega$ is countable. 
Since $\Omega$ is countable, there exists an injection $g: \Omega \to A$. 
The image $g(\Omega) \subseteq A$ is a subset of $A$. 
We can push forward the well-ordering $\prec$ on $\Omega$ to $g(\Omega)$ by defining $x \mathrel{R'} y \iff g^{-1}(x) \prec g^{-1}(y)$ for $x, y \in g(\Omega)$. 
Thus, $(g(\Omega), R')$ is a well-ordered set whose domain is a subset of $A$, so it belongs to $W$. 
Let $\gamma \in \Omega$ be the equivalence class of $(g(\Omega), R')$. 
By definition, $(g(\Omega), R')$ is order-isomorphic to $(\Omega, \prec)$ via $g$. 
Therefore, $(\Omega, \prec)$ is order-isomorphic to a well-ordering in the class $\gamma$. 
But the proper initial segment $I_\gamma$ of $\Omega$ consists of exactly those order types strictly less than $\gamma$, which corresponds to the initial segments of $(g(\Omega), R')$. Thus $I_\gamma$ is order-isomorphic to $(g(\Omega), R')$, which implies that $I_\gamma$ is order-isomorphic to $\Omega$. 
This means the well-ordered set $\Omega$ is order-isomorphic to one of its own proper initial segments, which is impossible. 
This contradiction proves that $\Omega$ must be uncountable.

We have thus constructed an uncountable well-ordered set $\Omega$ such that every initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable, establishing the existence of a minimal uncountable well-ordered set without assuming the Axiom of Choice.
